items.title: How Not to Waste Your Life
items.description: “Let me not seem to have lived in vain,” the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe whispered on his deathbed, not realizing that the astronomical tables he was leaving behind would become the portal through which Kepler arrives at the laws of planetary motion; not realizing that the measure of an unwasted life is not what outlives it but how it was lived — how much integrity and authenticity and creative vitality filled these numbered days, these unrepeatable hours. items.title: Sleep and the Meaning of Life: Fernando Pessoa on the Existential Dimension of the Horizontal Hours
items.description: One of the most important things I have learned about living is that, in any life of purpose and creative vitality, you must be as religious and disciplined about your sleep as about your work. And yet one of the great self-betrayals of our culture is the way it wears the lack of sleep as a badge of honor on the lapel of the ego of achievement — the cult of productivity gone past the sacrifice of presence, sacrificing even that precious nightly absence of conscious thought and metabolic urgency

items.title: How to Be a Lichen: Adaptive Strategies for the Vulnerabilities of Being Human from Nature’s Tiny Titans of Tenacity
items.description: When I was a child, little delighted me more than the magical green garlands draping from the pine trees, which I made into wreaths and mustaches to roam the mountains of Bulgaria as a miniature Orlando. I had no idea that Usnea longissima is just one of more than 20,000 known species of lichen — almost twice as many as birds. items.title: How to Love the World More: George Saunders on the Courage of Uncertainty
items.description: "In a world full of people who seem to know everything, passionately, based on little (often slanted) information, where certainty is often mistaken for power, what a relief it is to be in the company of someone confident enough to stay unsure (that is, perpetually curious)."

items.title: How to Love: Legendary Zen Buddhist Teacher Thich Nhat Hanh on Mastering the Art of “Interbeing”
items.description: "To love without knowing how to love wounds the person we love."

items.title: Carl Jung on Creativity
items.description: The question of what it takes to create — to make something of beauty and substance that touches other lives across space and time — is one of the deepest, oldest questions, perhaps because the answer to it is so unbearably simple: everything. We bring everything we are and everything we have lived to every smallest creative act — every experience, every dream, every memory, every unremembered impression, every unconsciously absorbed influence. items.title: How to Keep Life from Becoming a Parody of Itself: Simone de Beauvoir on the Art of Growing Older
items.description: "In old age we should wish still to have passions strong enough to prevent us turning in on ourselves."

items.title: G.K. Chesterton on the Dandelion and the Meaning of Life
items.description: Recovering the "forgotten blaze or burst of astonishment at our own existence" alive in the back of our modernity-deadened minds.

items.title: Borges on How to Conquer Time
items.description: "Time is the substance I am made of. Time is a river which sweeps me along, but I am the river; it is a tiger which destroys me, but I am the tiger; it is a fire which consumes me, but I am the fire."

items.title: The Wild Iris: Nobel Laureate Louise Glück on the Door at the End of Your Suffering
items.description: "Whatever returns from oblivion returns to find a voice."

items.title: How to Bear Your Sorrows: Nick Cave on Integrating the Darkness of Loss with the Bright Ongoingness of Life
items.description: Few things in our culture are more wounding than the concept of healing — as if the pains and losses that we suffer are an illness, a malfunction of the psyche to be cut out like a tumor, rather than a natural function of being alive, of feeling life deeply and living it fully. All our sorrows have been wasted if we have not learned to suffer and to be surprised by the door at the end of our suffering, on the other wide of which is simply the world, which keeps on worlding. items.title: Epictetus on Love and Loss: The Stoic Strategy for Surviving Heartbreak
items.description: "Who is good if he knows not who he is? and who knows what he is, if he forgets that things which have been made are perishable, and that it is not possible for one human being to be with another always?"

items.title: From Mitochondria to Minds: The Illustrated Science of the Psychedelic Dream Called Life
items.description: Like consciousness, like music, like love, life itself didn’t have to exist — nothing in the fundamental laws demands it. The universe could have gone on lapping at itself as a horizonless sea of pure spacetime, black and lifeless as the inside of a skull. But, in a whisper that soon became a symphony, life arose to give us such ceaseless wonders as the ghost pipe and the ginkgo, the bowerbird and the eye of the scallop. items.title: Marcus Aurelius on the Good Luck of Your Bad Luck: The Stoic Strategy for Weathering Life’s Waves and Turning Suffering into Strength
items.description: "What happened could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on."

items.title: Notes on Complexity: A Buddhist Scientist on the Murmuration of Being
items.description: "You are this body, and you are these molecules, and you are these atoms, and you are these quantum entities, and you are the quantum foam, and you are the energetic field of space-time, and, ultimately, you are the fundamental awareness out of which all these emerge."
